name: foliage
summary: Growing things: the grass tuft at a boulder's foot, the leaves on a tree. Thin, cut out, and lit through rather than off.
why: Metallic 0.0 and roughness 0.90, the roughest thing here. A leaf has no specular
highlight worth the name at this distance; what it has is a slight sheen on a waxy
surface, and MU's foliage art is 32 pixels of olive with an alpha fringe. Anything
glossier reads as plastic, which is the standard way foliage goes wrong.
No grain, and this is the deliberate one. Every other material here gets a generated
normal, and on foliage that is actively harmful: the geometry is a flat card, the shape
the eye reads is the alpha cut-out, and embossing a texture across a card makes it look
like a photograph of leaves printed on a board - which is exactly what it is, and the
one thing the material must not point out. Flat normal, and the silhouette does the
work.
It always comes with a cut-out sheet. That is not enforced here because a material
cannot see its sheet, but a foliage island whose asset did not declare a cutout is a
mistake and will render as an olive rectangle.
Its normals are forced to point up, and this is the fix for the single worst-looking thing
in the town. MU builds a bush out of crossed cards standing on their edges, so every one of
their true normals points sideways - and a sun 63 degrees up the sky lights a sideways
surface at the cosine of 63 degrees, which is almost nothing. A thousand clumps of grass and
eighty trees came out as black silhouettes on lit ground.
Pointing them up is not a cheat, it is what every foliage pipeline does: the normal a leaf
card should carry is the one belonging to the canopy it is part of, not the one belonging to
the quad it happens to be drawn on. The quad is a drafting convenience and its normal is an
artefact of that convenience.
It is declared on the material rather than in the exporter because it is a fact about the
kind of surface: anything whose shape is its alpha has this problem and nothing else does.
Translucency 0.28, which is the answer to a canopy half in black. Once the normals point
up, every card in a tree faces the sun - and the cards above shadow the cards below, so a
tree came out with a lit crown and a black underside. That is what an opaque surface does
and a leaf is not one: it is a tenth of a millimetre of green held up to the sun, and what
reaches the shaded side of a canopy is mostly light that came through the leaves above
rather than round them.
Carried as emission from the sheet's own colour rather than as a lighting model, because
glTF has no transmission a game engine reliably reads and the shape of the answer is the
same: a leaf in shadow shows a fraction of its own colour instead of nothing. 0.28 is
enough that a shaded canopy reads as green rather than as a hole, and low enough that a
lit one is still visibly brighter than a shaded one - at 1.0 the tree would be flat art
again, which is what MU had and what this is not.
